Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to enter this debate. I think this is a subject that is very important and one that in the past has caused considerable hardship. I think of my own riding of Niagara Falls a number of years ago and the provincially regulated company by the name of Astra Trust. I am sure there are Members in the House who will remember that incident.
The common complaint among a number of the individuals in that case was that they bought certificates, had invested money with the company and thought that they were covered by the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation and the protection given under that particular Act. They assumed in dealing with this company that there were either federal or provincial regulations and laws in place that would protect their investment. They unfortunately found out that they in fact were not covered. The story did not have a completely unhappy ending since there was government assistance in that case, but it pointed out the need at both levels of government to act in a way that would help protect individuals from that circumstance.
I am pleased that this subject, as well as other issues within the financial sector, has been under review by the Government. I believe there has been substantial progress made in it.
The Government has already implemented a number of measures to enhance consumer protection. As part of the financial sector reform package contained in the December 1986 policy document, Bill C-42 and Bill C-56 received Royal Assent just over a year ago. I think they go a long way to addressing some of the concerns that many of us have in this particular area.
I suggest as well that the federal Government has addressed the problems not only with its jurisdiction, it has encouraged and participated in discussions with its provincial counterparts.
Financial Institutions
In the area of financial sector change, the Government has met the challenge. Bill C-42 is a good example. The House should reflect for a moment on what measures have been taken by the Government of Canada in this area. Bill C-42 has an extension of the ban on unauthorized presentations of the insurance status of member institutions or of deposits received by them to persons acting as agents of such institutions.
In addition, that Act includes the incorporation in the CDIC Act itself of an existing regulatory requirement that when institutions take deposits which are not insured they must indicate that fact in writing on the deposit in contract. That is a very substantial and important change so that people see on the face of the contract whether or not they are protected.
In addition, there is a new requirement that member institutions who solicit funds for investment on behalf of their investment company subsidiaries or any other non-member of the CDIC give notice to investors that such funds are not covered. These new measures are in addition to the existing prohibition against anyone, other than a member institution, from representing itself or other member institutions as being insured by the CDIC.
As Members are aware, the Government is currently in the process of implementing the remaining measures contained in the December 1986 policy document. Among other things, these measures will grant broader powers to federal financial institutions, enabling them to provide their clients with a much wider range of financial services. The Government views the formation of such groups as a healthy development for Canada's financial markets.
In addition to providing Canadians with more choice and convenience in obtaining financial services, the diversification of financial institutions into new lines of business should enhance their ability to meet the challenge of increasing international competition as well.
The Government is well aware of the potential problems that are entailed in trying to protect the consumer. Consequently, the need for additional measures to address potential problems has been recognized in the draft of the proposed new Trust and Loans Companies Act which was released on December 21, 1987. By expanding the powers of trust and loan companies to provide various sorts of financial services to their clients, the draft legislation would also enable the Governor in Council to make regulations imposing terms and conditions with respect to those activities.

The key issue which this motion addressed is, of course: How do we go about ensuring that consumers get the information which they need to make sound saving and investment decisions? This question has been in people's minds a great deal since the failure of the Principal Group in Alberta.
As Members of this House all know, the Principal Group affair falls entirely under provincial juridiction, given that none of the 127 companies that constituted the Principal Group was federally chartered or regulated. In fact, only one of the Principal Group compagnies-Principal Saving and Trust-was even a member institution of the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation, or CDIC.
Nevertheless, I agree with the mover of this motion that the federal Government has a constructive role to play in preven-tinig the types of misunderstanding that occurred all too frequently among clients of the Principal Group.
I am pleased to note that the Government has already taken significant steps in the last few years with these issues in mind. Even prior to the Principal Group failure, the Government implemented a number of measures to ensure that clients of CDIC member institutions received better information.
Several of these were implemented through amendments to the CDIC act in July of last year which banned the agents of member institutions from making unauthorized statements regarding the insured status of the institutions or of any deposits received by them; introduced a requirement that when institutions take deposits which are not insured, they must indicate that fact in writing on the deposit contract; and required member institutions who solicit funds for investment on behalf of their investment company subsidiaries or any other non-member to give notice to investors that such funds are not insured.
These new measures are in addition to the existing prohibition against anyone other that a member institution from representing iteslf as being insured by the CDIC.
As Members of this House are aware, the Government is also committed to implementing addidional consumer protection measures as part of its proposed financial sector reforms.
Mr. Speaker, those measures are especially relevant given the growing trend towards the "networking" of financial services that is financial institutions marketing other institutions' products. I agree with the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Hockin) when he says, on page 24 of his december 1986 policy paper, that additional measures are needed.
In particular, I agree that rules are needed to ensure that clients of financial institutions are always informed of which financial institution it is that they are actually dealing with and of the presence or absence of deposit insurance coverage on the investments they make.
In conclusion, the measure which the mover of this motion has proposed is one such rule. But it is only one of a number of possible mechanisms for accomplishing this objective. Moreover, it is far from a perfect solution to the problem at hand.
In fact, it could easily create as many new problems as it purports to solve. This is so because, as others have pointed out, it could mislead consumers into believing that there is only one kind of insurance coverage for deposits and deposit-like investments.
In spite of all this, I think that the mover of the motion has the right objective in mind. Therefore, while I cannot support the motion as it currently stands, I support his call for additional efforts on the part of both federal and provincial Governments to take co-ordinated action to prevent the reemergence of problems similar to those which arose in the Principal Group affair.

Mr. Speaker, this motion presented by the Hon. Member for (Kamloops-Shuswap), (Mr. Riis) raises a concern which is felt by a good many Canadians. Indeed, I believe the record amply shows that it is a concern shared by the Government, one which it has already moved effectively to address.
There can be no question that Canadians expect and deserve the strongest possible reassurance concerning the security of their deposits in our financial institutions. As has been pointed out in this useful debate, not all our individual investment decisions can ever be fully guaranteed. Nevertheless, the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation goes a long way in ensuring that our savings will not have disappeared when we go to collect them. It provides an essential level of consumer protection by insuring individual deposits up to $60,000 in our federally chartered banks and most trust and loan companies.
The CD1C certainly provides the cornerstone of our consumer protection system, but it is not the whole structure. The Quebec Insurance Board, for example, offers CDIC-like coverage in that province for deposits in loan and trust companies and caisses populaires under provincial jurisdiction. Other provinces have established a number of corporations offering investment and deposit insurance.
We are not just concerned with protecting what we think of as conventional savings deposits at the bank or trust company. There is the whole business, for instance, of annuities sold by the insurance industry. As we know, the Government is currently working with the industry to determine the most effective means of providing insurance for annuities similar to the coverage the CDIC provides for bank and trust deposits. We must also bear in mind that as a result of the Government's reform of financial institutions legislation, our financial sector can look forward to offering consumers the choice and convenience of a much broader range of products and services. These will be placed on the market through networking arrangements between financial institutions. They are likely to include, to give just one example, deposit-like instruments that are in fact insured, although not necessarily by the same agency that insures the institution that sells them.
In light of all this, I have no quarrel with the general principles underlying this motion. It seeks to improve consumer protection, and none of us are against that. However, the question to be asked is, would it effectively strengthen
Financial Institutions
measures the Government already has in place and is in the process of implementing? Or does it, instead, try to do right things in a wrong way and thus unnecessarily creates new problems?
Other Members have already pointed out some of the motion's deficiencies in this respect and I will not dwell on them. Everyone agrees on the necessity for harmonization and co-operation between the federal Government and the provinces, but this is not likely to be achieved by asking federal regulators to set rules in areas of provincial jurisdiction. There are also technical problems raised by the motion including uncertainty of the precise meaning of the term "insured deposits", bearing in mind the variety of deposit insurance agencies and plans to which I have already referred.
This debate has nonetheless served the useful purpose of highlighting the range of measures the Government has undertaken to improve consumer protection even as financial sector reform allows growth of new and innovative customer services. The Government has strengthened the arm of the CDIC through the new provisions which clarify when deposits are and are not insured. It is now a statutory requirement that deposit contracts issued by CDIC-insured member institutions and their affiliates indicate in writing when deposits are not insured under the CDIC. Non-members of the CDIC and all persons acting as their agents are prohibited from representing themselves as being insured by the CDIC.
The Government's draft trust and loan companies legislation, as well as the new legislation covering banks and insurance companies, will empower the Government to impose strict regulations on the operations of these companies to safeguard consumers. What I believe all this adds up to is that Canadians have every reason for having confidence in the soundness of our financial institutions in the new era of reform, and in the Government's determination to give first priority to the protection of consumer interest.
As you well know, Mr. Speaker, I am from the Province of Alberta. Over the past few years we have had our problems. We have had problems with the failure of the Canadian Commercial Bank as well as the Northland Bank. After much discussion and a great many hearings the Government moved to assist the depositors. The opposition Member who is putting forward this motion, as well as members of the Official Opposition, ridiculed the Government. They opposed the Conservative Government when we moved to protect consumers in both these cases. How they have changed their minds. They have done a 180 degree turnaround. Now they are even talking about the federal Government moving on the disastrous Principal Group problem that we have in Edmonton, Alberta.
The Principal Group comes under provincial jurisdiction. It is certainly not under the federal Government's authority. I do not see any reason why the federal Government should step outside its bounds of authority.

August 18, 1988
Financial Institutions
Over the past couple of years the Government has taken initiatives through Bill C-42 and Bill C-56. Bill C-42 strengthens the federal supervision of financial institutions. New powers will improve the ability of the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation to protect the interests of insured depositors and other creditors. Federal regulators will have a stronger and a clearer sense of powers to take control of financial institutions that are insolvent and that violate their regulatory requirements.
We have also passed Bill C-56, a Bill that strengthens legislation governing banks, federally regulated trust, insurance and loan companies. The Government is committed through this Bill to ensuring that federally regulated financial institutions remain sound and are competitive, both domestically and internationally. We have taken steps to support and improve consumers' deposits. We have addressed issues-not to say that there is not more to be done.
In speaking to this motion 1 am sorry that I cannot support it. I feel very strongly that the Government, through Bill C-42 and Bill C-56, has certainly moved into the area to assure consumers that they have absolutely more legislation governing banks and federally regulated institutions, and that the CDIC has certainly improved its mandate. There is now more supervision in terms of CDIC deposits.
I appreciate having the time to express my views. I am sorry for the problems that Alberta has faced over the past few years. Hopefully, the province can resolve the Principal Group situation. We look forward to consumers being assisted there.

Mrs, Suzanne Duplessis (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State (Science and Technology)): Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) for bringing this motion before the House. As many of my colleagues have already indicated, the question of consumer protection in this period of financial institution reform is of obvious concern to many people, I am sure that all of us, as Members of Parliament, have heard from constituents who are worried about the stability and safety of Canada's financial institutions, particularly given the high profile failures of certain institutions over the past decade.
These failures have had a high profile, of course largely because the underlying stability and safety of our financial system made them unusual-the exceptions to the rule. While their effect on the system and the economy has been relatively small, they must not be considered unimportant. They are not unimportant to a small investor or depositor who loses money. He or she does not want the two levels of Government to point fingers and assign blame; they want something done about the situation.
These incidents have pointed to flaws in the existing system which must be addressed by both federal and provincial governments. I say federal and provincial governments, Mr. Speaker, because as you know, jurisdiction in this area is
shared. As the motion before us indicates by calling for co-operation between levels of governments, neither the federal Government nor provincial governments alone can protect the entire financial system.
The Federal Government has given top priority to protecting the consumer. In fact, it has been one of the most important principles guiding the Government's reform of the financial sector ever since it first came out with its Green Paper in the spring of 1985. Indeed, on the very first page of that discussion document the Government committed itself to nine principles designed to better serve the public interest in the regulation of financial institutions in Canada.
The principles are as follows:
-to improve consumer protection;
-strict control of self-dealing;
-to guard against abuses of conflicts of interest;
-to promote competition, innovation and efficiency;
-to enhance the convenience and options available to consumers in the market place;
-to broaden the sources of credit available to individuals and business;
-to ensure the soundness of financial institutions and the stability of the financial system;
-to promote international competitiveness and domestic economic growth; and
-to promote the harmonization of federal and provincial regulatory policies.
The Government re-affirmed its commitment to these principles in its Blue Paper tabled in the House in December 1986. These principles have guided the Government's actions ever since and, as indicated by its position on the list, consumer protection has been given top priority.
Mr. Speaker, a number of my colleagues have already pointed out the many ways in which the Government has strengthened and improved consumer protection. They have set out very well the measures it plans to introduce to further improve protection in the future. I am not going to spend the valuable time of the House in yet another recitation of these measures.
Let me just say about this that I believe the Government has done a lot to protect consumers, and should be congratulated for its work rather than receiving concealed criticism for not going even further. That does not mean that we cannot do more. 1 know that I am always interested in hearing about new ways to help consumers, as I am sure are most of my colleagues. However, although I can agree with the principles behind the Hon. Member's motion, that reflect in certain ways the principles I outlined earlier, 1 believe there are a number of problems with the motion.
There would be a number of difficulties involved in drafting a waiver form to take into account all the different kinds of
August 18, 1988

situations facing consumers of financial products today. As the borders between financial institutions become increasingly blurred, the difficulties would worsen. Even now it is difficult for a financial institution to know when a person's deposits exceed $60,000; for example, the client may have many different accounts located in various branches of the same institution.
There is also the difficulty of defining accurately the term "insured deposit". After all, there are many different kinds of deposit-insurance agencies, including: the federally chartered Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation, which insures federally chartered banks and most trust and loan companies; the Quebec Insurance Board, which offers similar coverage in Quebec for deposits in loan and trust companies and Quebec-registered caisse populaires; the Corporation du fonds de securite de la confederation Desjardins; various provincial "equalization funds" and investment-insurance and deposit-insurance corporations; and, compensation plans for holders of annuities and life and general insurance policies that are presently under discussion.
The situation becomes increasingly complicated when you consider that, in the future, financial institutions will be able to provide their customers with a much broader range of financial products and services. These could include instruments that are insured, but not by the same organization that insures the institution doing the selling. The possible complications along this line are endless.
The points I have made are only a few of the problems I foresee in trying to implement the Hon. Member's motion. But, as I indicated earlier, the general principles behind the motion-strengthening consumer protection and encouraging federal-provincial co-operation-are shared by the Government.
As the NPD House Leader pointed out in his opening remarks in February, his initiative is only one way of dealing with the issue of increasing consumer protection. Indeed, he admitted, and I quote: "There may even be other better ways of dealing with it." I believe this debate has revealed that the government has found better ways of dealing with the problem and has either implemented them or is in the process of implementing them.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS ADVISABILITY OF INFORMING DEPOSITORS WHEN DEPOSITS ARE UNINSURED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank the House Leader of the New Democratic Party, whose motion we are debating this afternoon, for giving me the opportunity to speak on the important and timely issue of better protection for depositors and investors in Canada's financial institutions.
The motion states:
That, in the opinion of this House, the Government should consider the advisability of co-operating with the provinces in establishing a system whereby those individuals who deposit money in financial institutions not covered by deposit insurance be required to sign a waiver form indicating that
Financial Institutions
they are fully aware that their deposits are not insured in the event that the
institution goes bankrupt.
In slightly less complicated terms the motion simply states that we improve our consumer protection and regulations, and that we co-operate and consult with the provinces in order to do so. This could be described as a motherhood issue. Everyone, particularly members of the Government, is in favour of ensuring that depositors and investors can continue to have a high degree of confidence in our financial institutions. We all want to know that our money is safe and that our banks and other deposit taking institutions will continue to be world class in both their levels of security and in their service to the public.
In these fast moving times, particularly in the financial sector, the issue is even higher in the minds of many. I can certainly understand the concerns of many Canadians when they read about the failure of some of our financial institutions.
Those of us who were elected for the first time in 1984 from the Province of British Columbia had barely been in office when we were approached by people who had invested their life savings in the B.C. Teachers' Investment and Housing Cooperative. It is a tragedy of tremendous dimension for people whose hard earned life savings are invested in any enterprise, whether it is a co-op, a business venture, or a bank. Many of these people were retired and their opportunity to earn was clearly diminished. They were dependent upon the investment that they had made and the deposits that they had in these institutions for their well-being. To lose them, by some freak combination of circumstances beyond their control, was a shattering blow to them. The hurt, harm, and in many cases the ill health that resulted from this failure, was of tragic dimension.
Consequently, federal and provincial Governments must do what is reasonably possible to assure Canadians that the financial sector, whether federal or provincial, is as strong and safe as it can be made.
However, ladies, gentlemen, and colleagues, there is no question that business ventures are exactly that; risks are taken, investments are made, and there is no guarantee in this world that all business investments will be successful. As parliamentarians we have to determine what is the proper role for us in trying to safeguard innocent Canadians without being so heavy-handed in a bureaucratic sense in attempting to indemnify for each and every possible risk that might come that indeed business is stifled itself. That is why debate such as this is important.
It is very clear that the present Government places a high priority on revamping our financial institutions to provide the safety measures that we all believe desirable. I personally feel much more assured by the measures the Government has taken over the past several years. 1 hope other Canadians will also feel that their money is safe and will continue to be safe in this period of financial sector reform.

August 18, 1988
Financial Institutions
No matter how hard we try, it is very difficult to legislate common sense. If an individual is determined to invest money, in the first instance that individual must assume some responsibility for checking out what it is that they are doing with that money. We can pass all the rules we like in Ottawa, but an investor who does not bother to read the big print, never mind the fine print, makes it very difficult for us as parliamentarians to save them harmless from all the things they might choose to do.
I am not going to repeat what a number of my colleagues have already said about the many ways in which the Government has and is strengthening and improving consumer protection. Nor will 1 reiterate the numerous problems and difficulties in implementing the Hon. Member's motion. Many of my colleagues have also pointed out that the Government has important and far-reaching plans for further improved protection, and they have adequately described those plans. 1 believe it would be a waste of your time, Mr. Speaker, and that of Members of the House to go over them one more time.
I would like to add my assurance that the Government has always, and will always, put the protection of Canadian consumers uppermost in its financial reform plans. We have also co-operated and consulted extensively with the provinces to better harmonize financial regulations across the country. This is consistent with what the Government has been saying about financial reforms since day one.
In the Agenda for Economic Renewal which was presented by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) shortly after we came to office, we discussed directions for change for the regulation of financial institutions. We stated: "The Government intends to respond by working with the provinces, the public and the financial community to ensure that legislation reflects the rapidly changing financial sector. Among the objectives must be the efficient delivery of financial services, while maintaining adequate protection for investors and savers, and intergovernmental harmonization of the regulatory framework".
If one reads the Government's original Green Paper on Financial Sector Reform, it is clear that protecting consumers has been a top priority for the Government. Indeed, on page 1 of that document the Government listed nine principles which would guide us in planning new directions for our financial sector. All nine principles were designed to ensure that the public would continue to have confidence in our financial sector while, at the same time, ensuring that the sector would remain strong and competitive internationally and could offer consumers more and better services.
Our number one principle was "To improve consumer protection"; as I said before, we have been consistent.
Our other eight principles were as follows: to strengthen the controls against self-dealing; to guard against abuses of conflict of interest; to design a financial sector policy that promotes competition in the sector, while enhancing innovation
and improving efficiency; to ensure that customers in the market-place will be able to choose from a wider array of options and new services and that the trend toward more convenience for consumers would continue; to broaden the sources of credit available to individuals and to businesses; to ensure and enhance the soundness and stability of the financial system; to promote the international competitiveness of our institutions while ensuring that they can continue to aid domestic economic growth; and, finally, to promote the harmonization of federal and provincial regulatory policies.
We have reiterated these principles and reaffirmed our commitment to them in the Blue Paper that we tabled in the House of Commons in December, 1986. We have been guided by these principles since.
It is clear that what the Hon. Member wants to achieve with his motion-and it is a laudable motion, namely better consumer protection and federal-provincial co-operation-is exactly what the Government is already working to achieve. Indeed, when he introduced his motion last February, the Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) pointed out that there may be better ways of dealing with the issue.
That remains to be determined. The Government is working energetically to find those safeguards. I had the privilege very recently of hosting the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Hockin) in my constituency of Esquimalt-Saanich. During his visit I arranged meetings for him with the banking community, members of the co-operative institutions and members of the trust companies to review the safeguards that we are discussing here today.
Part of the meeting was spent with my MLA in the Province of British Columbia, who also happens to be the Minister of Finance in the provincial Government. We discussed at some length the various kinds of institutions and the measures that this motion proposes.
I congratulate the Member for bringing forward this idea. It has to be very seriously considered, but as part of an over-all comprehensive review. It is one thing for us to pass rules here; it is another matter to legislate common sense. People have signed documents and have unhappily found, to their sorrow, that they really did not read what they had signed and did not know what they were signing, so it is difficult for us as legislators to indemnify citizens from many of their own actions when they choose to invest their money.

As I said earlier, I share the concern with respect to Motion 143 of the Hon. Member with respect to the issue of consumer protection in the financial sector. As he is well aware, however, the Government has given this issue a high priority as part of its financial reform package announced in December of 1986. For well over a year the Government has been dealing with this issue directly.
You will recall that last summer two separate pieces of legislation which strengthened consumer protection in the financial sector were passed and proclaimed. First, Bill C-42 made it a statutory requirement for CDIC insured institutions to indicate in writing on the deposit contract when they take uninsured deposits. That was a very good public policy and Parliament agreed with it.
The legislation cleared up the confusion surrounding the prohibition of non-members of the CDIC from representing themselves as being insured by the CDIC. That prohibition applies to institutions and all persons acting as their agents. The legislation goes further. CDIC insured institutions that solicit funds for investment on behalf of their investment company subsidiaries or non-members of the CDIC must give notice to investors that such companies are non-members and that such funds are not insured by the CDIC.
Second, another Bill, Bill C-56, introduced minimum capital requirements for life insurance companies. That will push the insurance industry to develop new forms of insurance to cover deposit-like instruments in the industry. The work is still in progress but it will result in coverage for insurance company annuities similar to the coverage for deposits provided by the CDIC. I am sure you would agree that the solution coming from the private industry where people work 24 hours a day would be much better than us as Members of Parliament trying to impose something from Ottawa. As we all know, we simply cannot cover that myriad of human relations and interactions that occur out there and it is much better if the protection comes from the field rather than from Ottawa.
I can assure the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) that the Government is moving effectively to deal with potential consumer protection issues as they relate to the Government's remaining legislation on financial reform. That legislation will allow federal financial institutions to offer their
clients a wider range of financial services. In particular, financial institutions will be able to enter into networking arrangements. This will help financial companies to remain competitive at home and abroad. It will improve services to Canadians.
However, these developments also raise concerns with respect to consumer protection since the companies involved in the networking arrangement may not all be members of the CDIC. In view of this fact, the trust and loan companies legislation that we have drafted will enable the Government to make regulations imposing terms and conditions on the networking activities undertaken by these companies. Similar provisions will apply in the new legislation for banks and insurance companies.
I could go on because I have notes covering it, but I know my time has expired and there is another Member who would like to speak on this important issue.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS ADVISABILITY OF INFORMING DEPOSITORS WHEN DEPOSITS ARE UNINSURED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is another Member whose duty it is to speak on this issue.
The House of Commons works in wondrous ways. The idea presented to us this afternoon by the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) is quite simple. Maybe you would not get that from listening to the debate that has now been going on for something like four and a half hours, I believe. The idea is really simple. Someone walks into a deposit-taking institution, a bank or trust company, and puts his hard cash down on the counter. There is a general assumption there that that money will be covered by CDIC or it will be insured. However, there are certain circumstances when it is not insured and what the Hon. Member wants to make sure of is that a person should be told whether or not that particular deposit is insured. In order for them to know he wants them to have to sign a little form, a little waiver or something like that.
It seems to me like a pretty simple idea and all the pros and cons of that could be debated maybe in half an hour at best and then maybe we could have a vote on it. That is not the way the House of Commons operates, unfortunately. It seems like we must have five hours debate on this. I am sure that certain people within the Department of Finance and the Ministry of State for Finance are rather hoping that this matter will die on the Order Paper and then our friend can resurrect it in the next Parliament in the unlikely event he is re-elected.
Eventually, 1 think the idea will come to fruition. Certainly a lot of thought has been given to the whole idea of deposit insurance and making sure that people know what they are getting themselves into when they put that money on the counter.
It is evident from things that have happened in the recent past, with the bankruptcy of trust companies-Principal Trust is a good case in point which has been brought to our attention several times already-where people who thought or had every reason to believe that their deposit was insured found out that it was not. The usual reason was because the deposit was for a
August 18, 1988

term of more than five years. Occasionally it might have been when the deposit was for an amount in excess of $60,000. We have been in debate in this House before as to whether or not it might be a good idea to up the $60,000 amount of $100,000, which I believe it is in the U.S. That is something that I personally would favour.
However, when someone walks into a deposit-taking institution, very often there is a big sign up there, or a little sign somewhere, that they can see which says this institution is a member of the Canada Deposit Corporation. It gives everyone the expectation that the deposit is insured. Sometimes I think these signs can be misleading, not deliberately so, but it might be a good idea if on that sign it would specify which deposits are insured and which deposits are not. It would have to be done in not too small a print but a fair size print on that sign so that people know.
It is also surprising the lack of knowledge on the part of many bank or trust employees. When you ask them whether a particular deposit is insured or not, they frequently do not know the details.
Anyway, I see that I have successfully concluded my mission. It is now six o'clock and I look forward to debating the issue again when it next arises.

(b)	the activities, economic viability and ability to compete within a given sector of all companies doing business in Canada and the United States of America; and
(c)	agricultural pressures in Canada resulting from the agreement."
I want to speak most particularly about part (a), the adjustment impact on company workers and communities, and I will have a few words to say also about part (b), the economic viability and ability to compete.
On part (a), I am concerned with one of the major industries in Spadina and in other parts of Canada, the clothing, textile and footwear industries as a group. This is an industry which has been suffering in recent years from a defective policy of the present and previous Governments on international trade and some tens of thousands of jobs have been lost during the 1980s and are not being, for the most part, recovered.
One reason why this industry is threatened-and in fact, the Chairman of the SAGIT, Mr. Nygard, who took part in the negotiations, says that it is threatened and that it should be withdrawn from the agreement-is that the current tariff levels in these industries are well above the average level of Canadian duties and therefore there is a wide consensus that this industry will suffer severely by the trade deal.
In the clothing industry, there may be a few specialty firms that will do well, but in general, with a tariff of around 23 per cent, the trade deal cuts will have a serious impact, particularly on major employers who are producing standardized, high-volume clothing. Canadian plants working by licence from foreign-owned firms are expected to suffer seriously. In Ontario alone, it is estimated by the industry, by the labour movement and by the Government that there will be 20,000 jobs at serious risk. That is in the clothing industry.
In the textile industry, the tariff averages close to 17 per cent. When these tariffs come down, the industry will suffer serious loss, as it did when the Government removed the import restrictions on leather footwear. Industry estimates show that Canadian producers of man-made fibres and cotton, cotton/polyester yarns and fabrics will not be in a position to compete with American imports. In fact, imports accounted for about 32 per cent of the market in 1986, up from only 26 per cent four years before.
We had a trade deficit in this industry in 1986 of $635 million and it will get worse under the trade deal, especially for Ontario where close to 50 per cent of the firms are located. Many, many of the workers will be out of work.

Mr. Speaker, I want to speak particularly to Motion No. 19. This motion would delete Clause 9 which would give the federal Government the authority it needs to impose the wine and spirits chapter of the agreement on the provinces. 1 and my Party believe that Clause 9 should be opposed, in fact that the whole agreement should be opposed, on the grounds that it allows the federal Government to enter unilaterally into provincial jurisdiction.
The Mulroney Government has boasted about how it has created a new era of federal-provincial co-operation and understanding. Yet, through this trade deal with the United States it turns around and unilaterally attempts to intrude in a way the provinces, especially the Province of Ontario, are not willing to accept in an essential area of provincial jurisdiction. This is a strange way to carry out, in a more meaningful and effective way, co-operation between federal and provincial governments. As is the case in so many matters, the Government has been saying one thing but doing another.
In short, Motion 19 not only allows the federal Government to intrude unilaterally into provincial jurisdiction but upsets, as a result, the federal-provincial balance and, above all, sacrifices the Canadian grape and wine industry. It is not only the farmers who grow the grapes who are sacrificed but the thousands of people who work with them during harvest and the thousands of people who manufacture the machinery and supplies they use and sell them to the grape growers of Ontario and British Columbia primarily.
If this deal goes ahead it will, as I have said, sacrifice the Canadian grape and wine industry. It has been estimated that some 20,000 direct and indirect jobs connected with the wine industry will be sacrificed in Ontario alone and thousands more will be sacrificed in British Columbia. That is another case of the Government saying one thing and doing another. The Government has boasted unduly about the jobs that have been created since it came into power. It has not made clear exactly what it has done to create those jobs and I do not think the creation of those jobs has very much to do with the policies of the Government. In fact, we see an example in this trade deal of how the policies of the Government are not creating jobs but destroying them, not by the hundreds but by the thousands.
A spokesperson for Bright's Wines of Canada best summarized the wine provisions of the agreement on the CBC television program Venture last August 15. He said that
August 18, 1988

basically the agreement will allow the United States wine industry to dominate the Canadian market and that once that American domination is established, it is unlikely that Canadian wine consumers will see significant price reductions as a consequence.
In fact, my recollection of that program is that the spokesperson for Bright's Wines said that the price of wines, both Canadian and American, would actually go up as a result of this agreement. That is again a case of the Government saying one thing while its actions bring about quite a different result.
The Government has been boasting that because of its trade agreement with the United States, consumers would be able to purchase cheaper products. With specific reference to the wine industry, the Government said consumers would be able to purchase cheaper wine, both Canadian wine and wine imported from the United States. Yet, one of the most knowledgeable persons in the Canadian wine industry, the head of Bright's Wines of Canada, has said that consumers will have a rude surprise if and when this trade agreement goes into effect because instead of cheaper wines, wines will be more expensive. That is another example of the Conservatives saying one thing and, through their policies, actually bringing about something quite different.
If this deal goes into effect and the tariffs and other provisions which support the Canadian wine industry are eliminated, not only will consumers, according to the President of Bright's Wines, have to pay more for their wine but in the interim Canadian vineyards will have been pulled out and our wine producers will have been lost.
We must recognize that there have been sound reasons for the policies we have to protect our Canadian wine industry. These reasons are not linked with narrow protectionism. Instead, they recognize the higher costs of production in Canada due to the shortness of our growing season and our over-all climatic conditions.
The Tories may say that it is just too bad, that if we do not have the right climatic conditions and the right growing season we should not have a wine industry. However, we have these climatic conditions not only for the wine industry but for our entire agricultural sector. If we apply the Tory reasoning to our agricultural sector right across the board, the Tories are saying goodbye to Canadian agriculture. As far as the Tories are concerned, Canadian agriculture can go down the tubes. As far as they are concerned, Canada can go down the tubes. They say "Goodbye Canada", because this whole country has to live with the shortness of our growing season and our overall climatic conditions.
The Canadian wine industry is clearly one of the major losers through the Mulroney trade deal. Virtually all analyses made by industry spokesmen predict widespread job losses in Ontario and British Columbia. The trade deal talks about the tariffs being removed over 10 years. However, if I am not mistaken 50 percent of those tariffs are removed in the first two years.

He said: Mr. Speaker, I must agree with the Parliamentary Secretary for a change. This has been a long, long debate. It is a debate which started, as the Hon. Member for Esquimalt- Saanich (Mr. Crofton) noted, in 1985. It is a debate which has continued with different permutations, different combinations, right up to the present. At each stage it has been a debate which has been characterized by the overbearing arrogance of the executive powers of this Government.
It was clear right from the start that this Government did not wish to debate this issue. It did not wish to develop a consensus in the country on something as crucial as this matter. Instead, it wished to direct its own path and to ram through its own policies. We can trace through the different steps by which this was done.
We can take, for instance, the committee, which the Hon. Member for Esquimalt-Saanich referred to earlier this afternoon, the committee which met in 1985, crossed the country and talked to far, far more people than any committee has yet had a chance to talk to. It found tremendous divisions on the issues of the trade deal. It also found some remarkably strong suggestions which were put to us by farmers, by people in the auto sector, by people who had concerns about the cultural sector, a vast range of people. Every single one of those recommendations was ignored. The committee said that the Auto Pact should be exempt entirely from negotiations. That suggestion was ignored. It was suggested that agriculture be left entirely out of the negotiations. That, too, was ignored. It was suggested that cultural industries be completely exempt. That, as well, was ignored.

Despite the fact that the committee said that this is the direction in which to go, that was ignored. It also said: "Don't jump right into a comprehensive trade discussion. Instead, talk about the present disputes which face us. See if we can work some of those out. We can talk, too, about the possibility of a comprehensive trade deal". We opposed that. The Liberals supported it. Nevertheless the point was that the approach was to be a step by step approach. That was rejected by the Government.
That was step number one, the first time in which the Cabinet said: "No, we will do it our way. We will decide. We will not follow what a parliamentary committee has suggested".
Then, we went to a second round of detailed considerations in the Standing Committee on External Affairs and International Trade. It made some very striking commitments. It said, among other things: "We agree, all of us-New Democrats, Liberals, Conservatives-that if the United States puts through its omnibus trade Bill without exempting Canada, then we should not take part in this trade deal with the United States". It was an absolutely clear-cut, straightforward conclusion.
What happened? The United States this summer passed the omnibus trade Bill, did not exempt Canada and the Cabinet nevertheless said: "Well, so what? A parliamentary committee has said the opposite but despite that we will take the direction that we want to take". The same thing has been true at each stage of debate with respect to this issue.
At each stage of debate, rather than allowing Members of Parliament to debate this issue fully and completely because it is so important to Canadians in every region and occupation, closure has been applied. It was applied at second reading. At the legislative committee stage there was a deadline put on the committee itself and its capacity to work. There was also a motion passed preventing that committee travelling across the country to hear people.
When we returned to the House of Commons for report stage and third reading, once more the Cabinet moved and stated that it would not permit Parliament to debate this fully. Instead it applied time allocation, cut the debate off, stopped the opposition members from making the very valid effective criticisms that they had been making, and forced this Bill through as fast as possible.
What is striking is that when one actually looks at the Bill, there is the same philosophy of the Cabinet knows best, and the Cabinet unilaterally will decide and direct what is best. Despite parliamentary reform, despite new approaches to our role as legislators, throughout this Bill in section after section it is the Governor in Council, i.e. the Cabinet, that will make recommendations, appointments, establish conditions, and that will set up committees. As a consequence, what we have is the worst possible insult to the Parliament of Canada that could
possibly be conceived of in a single Bill. There are dozens of places in this Bill in which the Cabinet unilaterally, without Members of Parliament having any say in the matter, will make decisions which will shape what happens to this country in the future. We who represent the people in their millions throughout the country will not have a voice even in the House of Commons to deal with these various decisions which the Cabinet can make unilaterally.
It seems to me that that is simply unacceptable in an age of parliamentary reform, it is unacceptable from any democratic perspective, and it is unacceptable in terms of permitting the participation of people to be fully and completely there in this whole set of crucial areas that the Bill deals with. That is why we have moved this set of motions which attempts to do two things. The first is to see to it that the Governor in Council, i.e. the Cabinet, has to report to and have its regulations, appointments, or establishment of committees approved by a committee of the House of Commons. If it is not approved by a committee of the House of Commons, then it has to come to the full House of Commons and there it has to be debated and approved by all Members of Parliament.
What we are talking about here is something which has become foreign to the Conservative Party ever since it took power, and something which becomes more foreign the longer it is in power. We are talking about the re-establishment of parliamentary democracy in this system. That is what these motions are about. 1 hope everybody in the House of Commons, with the possible exception of the Cabinet, will see the necessity of voting in favour of amendments that put constraints on the Cabinet's role to unilaterally and undemocratically shape the future of the country.

Mr. Speaker, I want to say at the outset that our Party will support these motions to amend the trade Bill because they are targeted at a very important and serious trend that has emerged over the years and which the whole trade deal simply exaggerates and emphasizes. Political scientists in this country have called it "executive federalism". It is increasing power that has been taken over by Members who hold executive office, escaping the responsibility to be accountable to Parliament, escaping public exposure and examination of their actions, making decisions behind closed doors, making decisions that do not have to be explained to anybody, and making decisions based on their own arbitrary discretion.
In part that is a natural consequence of a modern government. There is so much going on in so many places, obviously not all things can be examined in the House in a microscopic manner. However, that trend has not been a slow evolution as it was over the years, but it has become a galloping acceleration under the present Government.
The most egregious example is the Meech Lake Accord where executives of the 10 provincial governments and the federal Government met behind closed doors and changed the
August 18, 1988

Constitution without referring it back to the elected representatives of the people. They simply decided that this was good. No one can necessarily argue with that type of decision, but what many people reacted to was not the decision itself, but how it was made. It was the fact that people could assume unto themselves that type of almost unchallengable power to make these decisions.
When one looks at the legislation, the trade agreement substantially expands in all kinds of ways the executive power of the Government to make decisions which affect virtually all aspects of Canadian life, and they do not have to answer to anybody. They can sit inside the cabinet room, pass an Order in Council, get it gazetted about a month later in a whole pile where people have a hard time looking for it. One morning one wakes up and says: "My life has just been changed by the Cabinet and the trade agreement and 1 did not know anything about it".

amendments attempt to reduce the damage of the trade agreement.
Certainly we are very opposed to the very principle of the sell-out of our autonomy and the loss of the political power that is the constant theme throughout the trade agreement, Bill C-130. These amendments attempt to bring back a bit of a political review to give the House of Commons and parliamentary committees a chance to look at some of the rules and appointments that will very much affect how different bodies which deal with the free trade deal, should it go through, will operate.
The deal is all about getting rid of political power, getting rid of the power of a community to elect representatives to make decisions on its behalf and to see them implemented. The trade deal binds future Governments, cuts away from the scope of political decision-making and says that it will be determined by market forces, by a dispute-settlement panel and by the United States-Canada trade commission. These bodies of experts or these very diffuse forces will make the decisions that were previously made by Members of Parliament who were responsible to the people, Members who can themselves be thrown out of office by their electors at the next election. This is an opportunity to bring back a bit of political review at least.
Let us look at Motion No. 24 which seeks to limit the vast power of Cabinet to make appointments without any kind of review. Motion No. 24 would make appointments to the Canadian contingent of the Canada-United States Trade Commission reviewable by a parliamentary committee.
This is very important because the United States Trade Commission makes all kinds of extremely important decisions. Its members are, in effect, the trade ministers and other appointees. They decide on things like monopolies. There is a section in the Bill, put there with scarcely any discussion across the country, which uses American terminology such as "monopolies". We do not call them monopolies, we call them social services.
This relates to things like medicare, and whether we are going to have a national child care system. Suppose we want to extend medicare to include denticare or pharmacare. Suppose we want to do some other things as a community. If a company in the United States which is making money in health insurance does not want us to have medicare or does not want it to be extended in some way complains, the matter will go to a dispute settlement panel. The dispute settlement panel has a process to go through and its report goes to the commission, which accepts it or rejects it.
Who is on that commission and who is on those dispute settlement panels? Those are very important questions. Those are the kinds of bodies which will decide whether or not we can
have medicare or whether we will be forced to pay compensation in order to have it, which would make it prohibitively expensive.
These are the bodies that will make the crucial decisions which heretofore were made in Parliament or the provincial legislatures. There is terrific interference with the rules of provincial legislatures in the social sector and regional development in their own provinces. Municipalities which want to create jobs or start new social services could also be dealt with as infringing upon the future profitability of American corporations and could be subject to a challenge in the monopoly section.
If we ever have Indian self-government in this country, which I sincerely hope we will, the Indian bands will lose their power under the trade agreement to make all kinds of decisions on job creation, promotion of tourism, and starting their own social services. In effect, it is one of these bodies which we are reviewing in these motions that will decide whether or not they can do that. It is, therefore, very important who will be on these bodies.
In the case of the dispute settlement panel there will be five people; two Americans, two Canadians, and one to be appointed by those four people. Crucial decisions affecting our welfare system and regional development system will be made by supposed technical experts in trade matters. The majority will probably not be Canadians. If the four people have trouble selecting the fifth, that person will be selected by lot from a list. We could have three Americans and two Canadians deciding upon an absolutely crucial principle of Canada's social welfare system. This is an appalling abrogation of responsibility which will bind future governments.
If the present Government does not want to start a national child care scheme or to improve medicare, it is entitled to make those decisions. It was duly elected and for five years we suffer the consequences, then the voters have the chance to throw the rascals out. That's politics, that's parliament. With this agreement it is not enough just to throw the rascals out because the decision-making power has been taken out of parliament and cannot be reinstituted.
In the case of this Government we have the example of foreign investment review. The Government has substantially diminished foreign investment review, and the free trade agreement will diminish it further. Only the very largest corporate takeovers would be subject to investment review under this trade agreement.
If we elect another government on the platform of bringing back foreign investment review as part of the way in which to stimulate job creation in Canada, because of this free trade agreement it would not be able to do that. That political power will be lost and future governments will be bound by this trade agreement.
That is why it is so patently unfair for it to be rushed through against the will of provinces which disagree and with

no mandate from the people. This is so flagrantly immoral that I am surprised that the Government has the nerve to proceed. It does not have the nerve to take it to the public in an election.
The provisions in these motions do not make it impossible to have Conservative patronage in these appointments. We know that review by parliamentary committees does not stop Conservative patronage appointments. I have sat on committees. They are dominated by Conservatives who bring in their hack friends. The hack friends are asked token questions by the Conservative members and at the end of the discussion decisions are made by a majority. With government Members making up that majority, the appointment will go through. There is, therefore, nothing in here that will guarantee an end to patronage appointments. It is only when the public throws this Government out of office that we will have an end to that. 1 hope we will see that very soon.
However, these motions do not guarantee what we would like to have guaranteed. They do not undo the damage of the trade deal, but they do give Parliament a little bit more scrutiny. They do give the elected Members of Parliament, the people who are responsible to the public and could be thrown out at the next election, a bit more of a chance to do their job. The trade experts on the dispute settlement panel cannot be thrown out at the next election. They are appointed experts and are not responsible people. That is a violation of our parliamentary principles. I support these amendments because they at least provide for a bit of review of this corrupting practice although the far more desirable thing would be to get rid of the trade deal entirely.

That of course is baloney of the sort for which he is well known. It deals with all kinds of things, including the takeover of Canadian investment businesses and Canadian services such as management health services and so on. Nothing at all of those things relate to tariffs. In fact, for most people who work in the service industry-two-thirds of Canadians-tariffs are of secondary importance. So 80 per cent of trade is without tariffs. We will do away with the other 20 per cent. That will affect some of the manufacturing people. But the takeover of Canadian services will affect far more Canadians than the destruction of our manufacturing industry.
However, as could be expected, what the Hon. Member for Selkirk-Interlake was saying had nothing to do with the subject being debated at this time, namely, certain amendments that have been proposed by our Party. These amendments, roughly speaking, propose to introduce a measure of democracy into the operation of this new law in order to make up for some destruction of democracy.
Motion No. 24 proposes that appointments to the Canadian contingent of the Canada-U.S. Trade Commission should be reviewed by a committee of Parliament. Motion No. 33 proposes regulations regarding the operation of the procurement review board, the board that will decide whether the Government's policy of procuring goods is fair or unfair to the United States and that the implementation of the procurement chapter should be reviewed by a committee of Parliament.
The appointment of the Secretary to the Canadian Secretariat that will administer the dispute settlement panels and committees should be reviewed by a committee of Parliament. Orders and directives to the National Energy Board should also be reviewed by a committee of Parliament.
It seems by the excitement and anger of the Hon. member for Selkirk-Interlake and the Parliamentary Secretary that this proposal for democracy so frightens them that they had to talk about everything and anything else except the motions that are before the House at this time.
The Parliamentary Secretary taunts us not with debating. In fact, he does not debate. He just shouts, generalizes and tries to bulldoze. The point we are making is that government appointees who carry a huge responsibility for the conduct of the political economy of Canada and its relationship with the United States ought to have the approval, the scrutiny and the obligation to report to the elected representatives of the country-Members of Parliament.
Judging by their response to this proposal Members opposite think that this is some crazy, radical proposition; or they think it is something that could only be put forward by people who
August 18, 1988

have no interest in or knowledge of business. I point out to them that what we are proposing is no less than what is done by Constitution in the United States of America.
In the United States of America when the President appoints senior officials in various lines, his appointment must be validated, must be subject to the approval of Congress and Senate. There are a variety of regulations but that is the general principle. There are some times when his appointee is turned down, because the committee of Congress or Senate examine him and find him or her unsatisfactory, and the President must appoint somebody else. Tie has the power to name but not the power to put the person finally into office. We are suggesting that that development of democracy in the United States is something from which Canadians could learn, particularly if in this trade Bill we are going to have to do business with the United States. If they are good enough to do business with, if they are good enough for the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) to sing When Irish Eyes are Smiling with the President of the United States, then I think we could at least look at their structure for holding senior powerful officials to account before the elected representatives of the people.
That is what these amendments before us propose. They are absolutely essential if we are not going to lose a great deal of the more informal kind of democracy that we have now. The informal democracy that we have now meant that the executive of the Government, the Prime Minister and those he chooses to have in his Cabinet, ought to lay things before Parliament before final important decisions are made.
One example of that occurred about 30 years ago when the Government of the day under Mr. Diefenbaker negotiated the NORAD Treaty. The Leader of the Opposition, Mr. Pearson, said as a matter of Constitution it ought to be brought before Parliament. Mr. Diefenbaker agreed. It was brought before Parliament and voted upon. Unfortunately, Mr. Pearson and his successor in Liberal office forgot the rule that Mr. Pearson had put forward and this rule of course has been totally forgotten as well by the present Government. In fact, Mr. Pearson was right in 1958, and so was Mr. Diefenbaker, in putting that treaty to a vote of Parliament. There is no written law that says they must, but it was an essential obligation of democracy.
We are asking for essentially the same principle here. As I say we are following a very useful model in the United States of America that, when these officials are appointed, they should first be subject to an examination, a questioning by a committee of Parliament. If the committee does not approve their appointment, then it has to come to the full Parliament. If the Parliament does not approve their appointment, then the Prime Minister has to find somebody else who would be more acceptable.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Motion No. 31 that we are debating states that:
This section shall not come into force until equivalent and effective bid
challenge procedures arc available to Canadians in the United States,
It is a situation in which the Conservative Government and its weakling negotiators gave away an advantage to American corporations in Canada without getting an equivalent procedure for Canadians in the United States. One of the basic ideas behind a trade agreement is that we would have access. The reason the Conservative Government gave for pursuing this bilateral trade agreement with the Americans was new business opportunities for Canadian corporations in the United States. It was for access to markets, the reduction of tariffs, the elimination of retaliation through tariffs, quotas, countervail measures, as well as a dispute settlement mechanism. All of these were supposed to give advantages to Canadians that we did not heretofore have.
When we read the fine print we find out that there is no equivalency. Americans get advantages in Canada for which there is nothing remotely comparable, even on paper to what was given away.
In other clauses of the Bill, as in other parts of the agreement, there is all kinds of equivalency on paper. There is the level playing field on which the Americans have the same access to our energy resources as we will have to their energy resources. We will be able to get water from Arizona on the same basis as Americans will be able to get water from us. There is this theoretical, very abstract equivalence in many respects in the trade agreement. Yet it is not at all an equivalence in reality. This deal is entirely skewed to the United States. The Americans had their list of objectives with which
they did very well. The Conservative Government got precious little on its modest list of objectives. It did not even get some of the most important items on its very reduced list.
There is phoney equality on questions of energy security and things like culture. Either party can retaliate if the other party wants to use certain measures to promote culture for that party.
The United States does not need any particular measures to promote and protect its culture. It has vast markets which spill over into Canada. There are these so-called equivalent measures by which either party can do what it wants to protect its own culture, and the other party can retaliate. If Canada takes any steps forward to promote independent Canadian culture, the United States will retaliate. It will not work any other way.
The American Government does not need a CBC, a Canada Council or a National Film Board. It has a private sector in such vast markets that it does not need state institutions to do those things. We do not have any choice in Canada. If we are going to develop our Canadian culture we need to develop our own institutions. Our population is not large enough. We have two major language groups and a population that is spread across the country, with a greater cost of communication. We could not have done it any other way.
Therefore, there is this phoney equivalence in the area of culture and energy, so that the United States can protect its culture and Canada can retaliate, and Canada can protect its culture and the United States can retaliate. But we know how it will operate.
The Government does not care because it is so keen to link up with the neo-Conservative trends in the United States and to take advantage of them for its own gains in Canada that it is prepared to sell out. Where equivalency is provided, it is a phoney equivalency. The clause that is the subject of the motion before us does not even provide phoney equivalency as we have in culture, energy, or even monopolies where Canadian corporations dominating the health care system in the United States may threaten retaliation if the Americans brought in a medicare scheme. It is not very likely that the U.S. will bring in medicare. Canadian corporations do not dominate health insurance. That type of occurrence would not take place.
Where there is equivalency on paper, it is phoney. In this area, the Conservative Government did not even get paper equivalency. That is how callow it is at defending Canadian interests. It did not even get the same advantages for Canadians as the American negotiators obtained for Americans and their corporations.
This is a timid Government that wanted this agreement for the crassest of reasons. The Government was oriented to the sell-out. The Americans had tough negotiators with a very strong list. They sought and achieved what they had on their list.
August 18, 1988

They also managed to protect the areas that they wanted to keep to themselves. They did not want Canadians to get into American shipping, so shipping was wiped out.
The Americans use the arms industry as a major means of regional development. They have a very large military industry and arms production industry in the United States. It is a major way of producing jobs in particular disadvantaged areas. Such an area is provided with a new arms plant, which produces jobs and spin-off effects in that community. Arms plants are entirely excluded from the agreement.
While I am not arguing that they should be in the agreement, or that we want to be in that business, it is an example of the American way of promoting regional development which has been protected. Yet the Canadian way of promoting regional development has not been protected. We do not promote regional development by establishing arms plants in certain areas. We do it with regional development plans, which are in trouble. They are unfair subsidies and may be thrown out of the window now or in the first five to seven years of negotiations about what constitutes subsidies.
A local government or provincial government that wanted to create jobs in a way that would fall under a monopoly category would be in trouble. The Canadian way of doing things has not been protected, yet the American way has been protected. There is no equivalency.

Let me read this amendment to Clause 14 into the record. Motion No. 31 states:
That Bill C-130 be amended in Clause 14 by adding immediately after line 40 at page 6 the following:
"(3) this section shall not come into force until equivalent and effective bid challenge procedures are available to Canadians in the United States."

August 18, 1988
Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement
There is already in the United States an equally effective bid challenge procedure. It is in place now. It is there. It is open to Canadian firms and entrepreneurs. They have equal access to it, as do American entrepreneurs. It is already in place in the United States. It is something new for us. The procurement provision of the section about which we are talking will not come into force until the Governor in Council is satisfied that the United States has taken satisfactory steps to implement the free trade agreement, including Chapter 13, which is the procurement section.
