speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am anxious to speak in this debate because motion no. 31, to amend Clause 14, touches on the crux of the debate which is: "Access to the U.S. market." Since the beginning of this debate, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and all those who support the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement, claimed that even if we lost our political and cultural sovereignty, even with all the inherent risks for Canada, the fact that we would have access to the U.S. market was worth it.
And now, Mr. Speaker, we have just.. . my colleague just gave a demonstration and despite what the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade (Mr. McDermid) just quoted, he forgot that the Canadian Federation of Independent Businesses said the exact opposite of what he said a few moments ago in the House.
Of course the Americans are protecting all their industries! For instance, the garment industry will not be able to sell, to export to the United States under free trade, as the agreement claims. Manufactured goods must have a certain material content and a certain percentage, so that not all Canadian garment manufacturers will qualify to enter the United States. So in fact, we are restricting access.
Mr. Speaker, the big surprise came after analysing the Bill and the entire document. Hardly a month ago, everyone thought small business was well protected and that a free trade agreement between Canada and the United States was a good thing to have. Now the Canadian Federation, which was actually advocating this agreement, has just said, and I will give you the direct quote later on Mr. Speaker, that there was no provision for allowing Canadian small business to bid on U.S. contracts. A thorough analysis of both the Canadian
Government's policy, announced wiht great fanfare not long ago, and the U.S. policy shows that we lose on both fronts.

A lot of people were surprised to hear criticism from the Canadian Federation of Small Business in The Financial Post of July 5, 1988, and I quote:
Canadian small businesses are unlikely to benefit from the $4 billion in U.S. Government spending available to Canadian enterprises under the free trade pact, the Canadian Federation of Independent Business says.
That is exactly opposite to what the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade (Mr. McDermid) said a few moments ago. The article continues:
American small businesses will receive preferred status over their Canadian counterparts when Washington allocates the portion of U.S. spending set aside for this category of business, CFIB Research Director Catherine Swift said in an interview.
Meanwhile, American small businesses can bid up to $400 million in annual Canadian Government spending provided for in the agreement without any Canadian preference as to nationality or size of enterprise.
We do not have any of these things to protect Canadian small businesses. Why do Americans protect their small businesses? If it is free trade, then why are we not treated equally? Why is there this difference? In the same article it is stated:
"We're not delighted with the government procurement provisions in the agreement," Swift said. "There's no advantage to small firms. It's likely to benefit large companies."
Swift's remarks came in the wake of news conferences yesterday in Toronto by Supply and Services Minister Otto Jelinek and Montreal by Bernard Valcourt, Minister of State for Small Business & Tourism.
They were trumpeting changes in federal procurement policies aimed at increasing the share of federal spending awarded to small business.
Jelinek pointed out that the free trade agreement allows up to $4 billion of U.S. government spending to be awarded to Canadian enterprises. That compares with a total of $8.7 billion allocated by Ottawa in contracts to all firms last year.
But Swift noted that U.S. law requires a certain portion of U.S. federal contracts must be set aside for American small businesses, leaving little if any-for their Canadian counterparts.
It is very clear that what the Parliamentary Secretary told us a few minutes ago really does not make sense. Since July 5 the Canadian Federation of Independent Business has defended the free trade accord as a bonanza for small business. This article is clear. It says that the procurement policy of the Canadian Government and the American Government in the free trade accord does not protect Canadian small business. It does not give anything to help that sector of our economy.
Last Tuesday the Minister of State for Small Business and Tourism (Mr. Valcourt) announced in a press conference, along with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. de Cotret), that they were creating an institute of entrepreneurship. They have sold the shop in terms of defence of small business. That
August 18, 1988

is what happened to small business. The institute of entrepreneurship has nothing. It has no budget and no mandate. That is how the Government is telling people that it will do something, when we look at the facts and read the fine print we see that there is nothing for small business.

Mr. Speaker, this is unfortunate, because we are talking about a sector that creates most of the jobs in this country. Ninety-two per cent of Canadian businesses are small businesses. When an agreement of this magnitude penalizes this sector, that is something we cannot accept. This sector, even during the recession, created more jobs than any other sector. How will the Government be able to protect small businesses in its negotiations with the Unites States? The Americans have protected their small business sector, but we did not protect ours, and that is unacceptable.
I strongly support the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy) who proposed this amendment which is aimed at protecting small business, and I urge all Members of this House to support the amendment as well because it is so important. If we can't protect small business now . . . How can the Canadian Government go off on a tour, which is what the Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism) (Mr. Valcourt) is doing, and tell people triumphantly that it is going to announce programs without budgets or funding or a mandate, when at the same time, in a free trade agreement of this kind, they completely overlooked small businesses in the section on government contracts and services, and many more sectors like the garment industry which, in fact, affects a large segment of small business?
I think it is clear, Mr. Speaker, that we must reject this agreement and support the amendment proposed by the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry.

It js crucial in this debate that we set out precisely wbat we see in the agreement, what therefore to us appears to be true and what therefore is something that the people of Canada should be concerned about as they consider the questions that are going to be discussed and debated in the election which is coming up and, of course, in the evaluation of this debate itself. The Parliamentary Secretary said that we do not have to worry about the United States because it already has effective bid challenge systems for prpcurement purposes which are in place.
Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement
I put the question to people who are watching this debate: If that is the case, if that is the reality, then why it is that Article 1305.3 states:
Each Party shall introduce and maintain, in accordance with the principles
contained in Annex 1305.3, equitable, timely, transparent and effective bid
challenge procedures for potential suppliers of eligible goods.
Why would it be necessary to have a commitment from the United States that it will introduce such an equitable, timely, transparent and effective system if in fact it already has such a system? Clearly, the people watching are going to realize that in this, as in other areas, the Government is trying to paint a picture which is not a true picture of reality, but a picture which in its implications for Canadians does not convey what is accurate.
For instance, if we look at a number of other points with respect to this whole exercise besides the procurement area, the Government said it would seek this trade deal in order to get an exemption from countervail. It said that specifically. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) in New York said specifically: "We want an exemption from countervail". It was also stated that we had to have a subsidy code on which we agreed as a key objective of the trade negotiation. Neither of those crucial and absolutely fundamental goals that the Government stated it wanted was achieved. That is one reason we are so dead set against the deal.
The other reason is that when one looks at the immense losses that this country gave up in the trade deal one realizes that we gave up the power to review takeovers of virtually any Canadian firm by American companies. It is now possible for an American company to take over a Canadian firm, shut it down, lose those jobs, and as a country we can do nothing about it. That is one loss.
A second loss is that it is no longer possible for us, when we have a shortage in energy in the future in natural gas, or electricity to redirect exports which we were sending to the United States. We can cut back, but we can only do so to the degree that we let the Americans have access to (he same proportion of energy as they had previously. That is the second loss.
The third loss is in cultural policy. We have given in print to the Americans something that they never have had before, the right to retaliate against us if we take action to protect our culture. Never in the past has a Canadian Government given that right in writing to the United States, yet this Government has done it.
Fourth, we have given up major concessions in health care. Under the agreement we have reached with the United States it is now possible for an American company to establish a hospital for profit in this country, and we cannot stop them. It is also possible for the United States to operate that hospital because it is a covered service. Therefore, it becomes possible for our health care system to be taken in a for-profit direction.

August 18, 1988
Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement
Chapters 16 and 14 of the agreement establish those conditions. Those are facts, those are realities, and they are a fourth area which we have lost.
We have lost major concessions with respect to the Auto Pact. It used to be protected by tariffs which would have to be paid.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one of the joys of being here on an August evening is listening to speakers such as the Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor (Mr. Langdon). In his normal fashion of addressing the Chamber he has featured a very reasonable analysis in tempered tones and clear logic. It is the type of speech when one hears it, if one accepts the step taken by the following step and the successive step, in which one can feel that there is a logic unfolding, the analysis is pristine and it is taking one to a new height of understanding, a new level of insight as to what is before us.
The true and profound pity is that this logic and fine thinking is misdirected because it begins with a false premise. It is like the rocket ship that is aimed for the moon. It may just be the slightest bit off as it leaves, but, by the time it gets there, it misses its target entirely. That is what I fear I have to report to my colleague, the Hon. Member for Essex- Windsor. Although it is a true joy to listen to him, by the time he reaches his conclusion one realizes that he has gone far astray. He ended off by saying that what we have in the free
trade agreement negotiated between Canada and the United States is "a totally unbalanced deal".
In the context of the amendment that we are debating here dealing with procurement review, there is a small example of the general thesis of how the New Democratic Party, of which the Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor is a spokesman, through its efforts to continually misinterpret so many of the facts that relate to this treaty between our two countries, has rendered such a gross distortion that members of the New Democratic Party may even have persuaded themselves that it is a totally unbalanced deal, but here is the fact and let us bring it into sharp focus on the amendment before us.
The purpose of the proposed amendment is to impose a condition on the implementation of the procurement review board. Motion No. 31 specifically states:
"(3) This section shall not come into force until equivalent and effective bid challenge procedures are available to Canadians in the United States."
In spite of what the Member has said on this issue a few moments go, as I say, step by step in his logical unfolding of the issue, he has overlooked the fundamental starting point, that there is already an equally effective bid challenge procedure in place in the United States to which Canadian firms and entrepreneurs have equal access. However, that is not all. There are sufficient safeguards in place in Bill C-130, and in the free trade agreement itself, to ensure that the United States will live up to its obligations under the procurement chapter. Specifically, the procurement provisions will not come into force until the Governor in Council-that is the Canadian Government, our Cabinet-is satisfied that the United States has taken satisfactory steps to implement the free trade agreement, including Chapter 13. Those are the Canadians who have the final say on this; the Government and the Cabinet of Canada.
For the Member to say that this is a totally unbalanced deal is to fly in the very face of the fact that the decision to be taken on this is the decision of the Canadian Government.

Hon. Warren Allmand (Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine
East): Mr. Speaker, we are presently debating an amendment to Bill C-130, the Canada-U.S. trade legislation, an amendment which deals with government procurement. If we look at the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement, in Chapter 13, which is the chapter that deals with government procurement, we will see that it provides that Canadian businesses will have access in bidding to certain types of government contract in the United States, and that American businesses will have the right to bid on certain types of government contracts in Canada. The provisions of Chapter 13 provide for a slight improvement with respect to access in bidding on government contracts than has existed up until now. I say a slight improvement. This chapter provides for this access to bid on these government contracts in both countries.
As you read through the chapter it states that each party, meaning Canada and the United States, shall introduce and maintain, in accordance with the principles contained in Annex 1305.3, equitable, timely, transparent and effective bid challenge procedures for potential suppliers of eligible goods. So it is saying in that article that both Canada and the United States should introduce and maintain bid challenge procedures for suppliers, that is, businesses which have complaints against the system of either country, complaints that they are not being treated fairly in accordance with the agreement.
What has happened as a result of that provision in the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement? As a result, Canada, in drafting its legislation, provided a Part II, entitled "Procurement Review Board", and they did just what was required in Article 1305.3 of the agreement. They did set up bid challenge procedures in accordance with that article. They set up a board to deal with the complaints of businesses, American businesses, which feel that they are not being fairly treated in accordance with the agreement in Canada.
Here is the Canadian Bill. It has Part II, dealing with this matter. Here is the American Bill, and if you look through it, there is no such provision. The Parliamentary Secretary and other government Members have said that there is no need for the Americans to provide a similar procedure in the United States because they already have similar procedures which existed long before this Canada-U.S. trade agreement was negotiated and agreed upon. That is what the Conservative Minister and the Conservative Members said.
When Canadian businesses look at this, they do not agree. This is not Liberals or Conservatives who do not agree with the Government on this; this is Catherine Swift, the Research Director of the Canadian Federation of Independent Business.

August 18, 1988
Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement
Catherine Swift disputes whether the provisions on government procurement will benefit Canadian small business. She has grave doubts whether the long-standing procedures in the U.S. really satisfy the requirements of the agreement as set out in Article 1305.3. This is reported in an article in the Financial Post of July 5, 1988, only a month or so ago. The article reports that Canadian small businesses are unlikely to benefit from the $4 billion in U.S. government spending available to Canadian enterprises under the free trade pact. American small businesses will receive preferred status over their Canadian counterparts when Washington allocates the portion of U.S. spending set aside for this category of business.
It goes on to deal with these particular matters and refers to the inadequacy of the American system to meet the needs of Canadian small businesses as opposed to the rights of American businesses when they are in Canada. As I say, that is because if you look at the American legislation it does not have the same provisions as the Canadian legislation. What they had in the past is open to doubt, not just by the Liberals and NDP but by the Canadian Federation of Independent Business.
In responding to us, the Parliamentary Secretary says we Liberals and New Democrats do not understand. We are not very smart. I guess he has to direct that allegation at the Research Director of the Canadian Federation of Independent Business as well. I think Canadians want to judge for themselves.
This is another example of the inconsistency or imbalance between the Canadian legislation and the American legislation. There are other things in the Canadian legislation to benefit Americans doing business in Canada which are not in the American legislation to benefit Canadian businesses in the U.S. If we in the Opposition had not campaigned for weeks and weeks against the former Article 8 which said that everything in this Bill and the free trade agreement would prevail over every other piece of legislation in Canada, we would have had a second Constitution. The American legislation had exactly the opposite. For months and months we tried to convince the Government that this was a very imbalanced approach. It was wrong. The Minister said week after week, no, it was not, and he would not do anything about it. Finally, I guess, he came to his senses and withdrew that article.
Of course, he took the same approach on water. He resisted and resisted, said it did not mean anything, and finally he put an amendment in the Bill to deal with export of water to the U.S.
One of the things that concerns Canadians is that when you put the American Bill and the Canadian Bill together, you do not find exactly the same provisions. Canadians are right in saying that if this is an agreement, surely the laws in both countries should be the same and have the same provisions.
Before I sit down I want to deal with a point raised in the debate by government Members. They said that if we oppose this agreement in principle, and if we oppose it in its entirety, why are we making amendments to different sections? They are accusing us of simple obstruction in doing that and of wasting time. The reason we are making amendments to many clauses of the Bill is to show how inadequate, how faulty, how completely wanting this piece of legislation and this agreement is. The only way we can do it is to go through it part by part, section by section, chapter by chapter, moving amendments, debating them, and thereby informing the Canadian public just how bad this free trade agreement is and why it should be rejected in its entirety.
